title: Cercospora Leaf Spot: How to Spot It and Stop It in Vegetables
metaTitle: Cercospora Leaf Spot: Signs and Control in Vegetables
metaDescription: Cercospora leaf spot makes round spots with dark edges and pale centers on vegetable leaves. Learn the signs, causes and steps that lower the risk.
excerpt: Cercospora leaf spot is a fungal disease that makes small round spots, with dark edges and pale centers, on the older leaves of vegetables. Left alone, the spots join, the leaves yellow and drop, and the crop yields less.

heroImage.alt: A leaf with many small round spots with pale centers, the signs of Cercospora leaf spot
heroImage.credit: Plant pests and diseases, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Cercospora leaf spot is a name for a group of related fungi in the genus Cercospora. Each one prefers its own crop. Cercospora citrullina attacks melons, watermelon and other cucurbits, and Cercospora beticola attacks beet, spinach and Swiss chard.

Cercospora fungi also live in the Philippines. Researchers at the University of the Philippines Los Baños recorded a Cercospora fungus on red Basella (alugbati) leaves in Laguna. I found no Philippine extension sheet that ranks the disease for local vegetables. So most advice here comes from university extension services that study the same fungi. The habits are the same in warm, humid weather. A tropical fact sheet on the pepper form shows the same pattern. Leaf spots on vegetables are often confused with [anthracnose](/diseases/anthracnose) or [early blight](/diseases/early-blight), so it helps to check the shape of the spot.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Cercospora spp. (for example C. citrullina on cucurbits and C. beticola on beet and spinach)
Cucurbits (melon, watermelon, cucumber), beet, spinach and other vegetables
It builds in warm weather with long leaf wetness, and it starts on the older leaves before it climbs the plant, usually once the crop has a full canopy.

The fungus survives in crop residue, seed and weeds. Rain splash, wind, tools and workers carry its spores from the old residue to the leaves, and each new spot makes more spores. On pepper, the Pacific fact sheet adds that the fungus can ride on the seed.

blocks.text: How to Identify Cercospora Leaf Spot

Start with the older leaves. The first sign is a small, round, light colored spot that grows and gets a dark margin, which can be red to purple on beet. The center turns white, tan or gray, and it may fall out and leave a hole. A yellow halo may circle the spot as it grows. In wet weather, the stems and leaf stalks can also be hit. Tiny black dots in the center of the spot are the structures that make spores.

items: Small, round spots appear on the older leaves first.
Each spot has a dark, reddish or purple edge, and a white, tan or gray center.
The center may drop out and leave a hole in the leaf.
A yellow halo may surround the spots, and many spots join into dead areas.
Heavily hit leaves yellow and drop, and the stem or leaf stalk may be spotted in humid weather.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Round spots with a pale center can look like [anthracnose](/diseases/anthracnose) on some crops. Cercospora spots start small and round on the older leaves, with a dark margin and a pale center.
How Cercospora Leaf Spot Hurts Your Crop

Cercospora leaf spot lowers the yield by killing the leaves that feed the crop, and it can spoil the look of leafy vegetables that you sell by the bundle. How much you lose depends on the crop, the variety and how long the leaves stay wet. I did not find a sourced loss figure for vegetables in the Philippines, so I give none. A tropical fact sheet on the pepper form says severe attacks join the spots and drop the leaves. It adds that fruit yield falls and that warm wet weather favors the disease.

The fungus survives in plant residue and in soil for up to 3 years, according to Cornell. So the spots you see this season often come from last season's leaves. Good sanitation costs little, and it works better than any spray. See our guide to [growing vegetables in the Philippines](/crops/vegetables-philippines).
How to Control Cercospora Leaf Spot

items: Space plants so the air moves through the canopy and the leaves dry fast after rain or watering.
Use drip or furrow irrigation, and avoid overhead watering when you can, since wet leaves are what the fungus needs.
Remove and destroy diseased leaves early in the season, and carry them out of the field.
Rotate with crops that are not hosts, for at least 2 years, for 3 or more years where beet or spinach is the host, and for at least 3 years after the disease has hit pepper.
Pull out weeds that act as hosts, such as lambsquarters and pigweed, which carry the beet fungus.
After harvest, destroy the crop residue by deep plowing so that the old leaves are buried and cannot send spores to the next crop.

blocks.text: Fungicides help best when they protect the leaves before the disease builds up. Extension services advise a protectant spray from the time the vines touch, and earlier in fields with a history of the disease. Some Cercospora fungi have become resistant to strobilurin fungicides in New York, so do not rely on that class alone. Follow the label of an FPA registered product, and rotate groups. Tamil Nadu Agricultural University lists copper oxychloride for the eggplant form. The Pacific fact sheet lists chlorothalonil, copper oxychloride and mancozeb for pepper.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Rotate away from the host crop for at least 2 years.
Use clean seed, and treated seed where it is sold.
Keep the field free of hosts, such as weeds in the same family.
Bury or remove crop residue straight after harvest.
Scout older leaves every week once the canopy closes, and start protection early if the field had the disease.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cercospora Leaf Spot

items.q: What does Cercospora leaf spot look like?
items.a: It makes small, round spots with a dark margin and a white, tan or gray center. A yellow halo may circle them, and the center can fall out.

items.q: Where does the fungus come from?
items.a: It survives in crop residue, seed and weeds. Cornell says it can stay in soil and plant residue for up to 3 years on beet crops.

items.q: Do I need to spray every season?
items.a: Not always. Spacing, drip irrigation, rotation and residue control come first. Spray only when the field has a history of the disease or the weather is wet and warm.
